Contract Explainer

Section 7 — Indemnification and Limitation of Liability

Plain-language summary and glossary for a non-technical reader

The Task

Request

Summarize Section 7 of the contract for a non-technical reader, and define the key legal terms in plain language.

Show the original contract text 
7.1 Mutual Indemnification. Each Party (the "Indemnifying Party") shall defend, indemnify, and hold harmless the other Party and its officers, directors, employees, and agents (the "Indemnified Parties") from and against any and all third-party claims, demands, actions, suits, or proceedings (collectively, "Claims") and all resulting losses, damages, liabilities, settlements, judgments, fines, penalties, costs, and expenses (including reasonable outside counsel fees) (collectively, "Losses"), to the extent such Claims arise out of or relate to (a) the Indemnifying Party's breach of any representation, warranty, or covenant hereunder; (b) the Indemnifying Party's gross negligence or willful misconduct; or (c) any allegation that the Indemnifying Party's Deliverables, when used in accordance with this Agreement, infringe or misappropriate any third party's intellectual property rights, provided that the foregoing (c) shall not apply to the extent a Claim arises from (i) modifications made by the Indemnified Parties, (ii) combination of the Deliverables with materials not supplied by the Indemnifying Party where the infringement would not have occurred but for such combination, or (iii) use of the Deliverables outside the scope expressly permitted under this Agreement.

7.2 Indemnification Procedure. The Indemnified Parties shall (a) promptly notify the Indemnifying Party in writing of any Claim (provided that failure to so notify shall not relieve the Indemnifying Party of its obligations except to the extent it is materially prejudiced thereby), (b) tender sole control of the defense and settlement of the Claim to the Indemnifying Party (provided that the Indemnifying Party shall not settle any Claim that admits liability of, or imposes any non-monetary obligation on, the Indemnified Parties without their prior written consent, not to be unreasonably withheld), and (c) provide reasonable cooperation at the Indemnifying Party's expense.

7.3 Limitation of Liability. EXCEPT FOR (i) A PARTY'S INDEMNIFICATION OBLIGATIONS UNDER SECTION 7.1, (ii) BREACHES OF CONFIDENTIALITY UNDER SECTION 9, (iii) A PARTY'S GROSS NEGLIGENCE OR WILLFUL MISCONDUCT, OR (iv) A PARTY'S INFRINGEMENT OF THE OTHER PARTY'S INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY RIGHTS, IN NO EVENT SHALL EITHER PARTY BE LIABLE TO THE OTHER FOR ANY INDIRECT, INCIDENTAL, CONSEQUENTIAL, SPECIAL, PUNITIVE, OR EXEMPLARY DAMAGES, OR FOR ANY LOST PROFITS, LOST REVENUE, LOSS OF GOODWILL, OR LOSS OF DATA, HOWEVER CAUSED AND UNDER ANY THEORY OF LIABILITY, EVEN IF ADVISED OF THE POSSIBILITY OF SUCH DAMAGES. SUBJECT TO THE FOREGOING, EACH PARTY'S TOTAL CUMULATIVE LIABILITY ARISING OUT OF OR RELATING TO THIS AGREEMENT SHALL NOT EXCEED THE GREATER OF (A) THE FEES PAID OR PAYABLE BY CUSTOMER TO PROVIDER UNDER THIS AGREEMENT IN THE TWELVE (12) MONTHS PRECEDING THE FIRST EVENT GIVING RISE TO LIABILITY, OR (B) ONE HUNDRED THOUSAND U.S. DOLLARS ($100,000).

The Short Version

In one paragraph: If someone outside this contract sues you because of something the other side did wrong, the other side has to step in, run the lawsuit, and pay the bill — and the same rule applies in reverse. In exchange, both sides agree to cap how much they can ever owe each other: no payment for knock-on business losses like lost profits, and a hard ceiling of either the last 12 months of fees or $100,000, whichever is larger. That cap does not apply to the worst categories of misconduct.

Clause by Clause

7.1 Who covers whom

Each side promises to protect the other from lawsuits brought by outsiders. "Protect" here means three things bundled together: hire the lawyers and run the defense, pay whatever comes out of it (judgments, settlements, fines, legal fees), and make sure the other side doesn't end up out of pocket.

This protection kicks in for three kinds of problems:

  • Broken promises. You said something in the contract and it turned out to be untrue, or you agreed to do something and didn't.
  • Serious misbehavior. Not ordinary mistakes — this covers reckless carelessness or doing something wrong on purpose.
  • Stolen or copied intellectual property. Someone claims the work you delivered uses their patent, copyright, trademark, or trade secret without permission.

The IP protection has three escape hatches. The provider is off the hook if the customer changed the delivered work, bolted it onto something else the provider never supplied and that combination is what caused the problem, or used it in a way the contract doesn't allow. In short: you're covered when you use the thing as intended, not when you modify it or go off-script.

7.2 The rules for asking for help

Protection isn't automatic — the side being sued has to follow three steps:

  • Tell them quickly, in writing. A late notice doesn't cancel the protection unless the delay genuinely damaged the other side's ability to defend the case.
  • Hand over the steering wheel. The side paying for the defense gets to run it and decide whether to settle. The trade-off: they can't agree to a settlement that admits you did something wrong, or that forces you to do something beyond writing a check, without your written OK — and you can't refuse that OK for no good reason.
  • Help out. Turn over documents, make people available, and so on. The other side reimburses you for the cost of helping.

7.3 The ceiling on what anyone can owe

Two separate limits, both written in capital letters because the law generally requires these to be conspicuous:

  • No ripple-effect damages. Neither side can claim indirect losses — lost profits, lost revenue, damaged reputation, destroyed data. Only direct, immediate harm counts. This holds even if the other side warned in advance that these losses could happen.
  • A total dollar cap. Everything either side could ever owe under this contract is capped at the higher of: the fees the customer paid (or owes) in the 12 months before the first thing went wrong, or $100,000. If 12 months of fees came to $40,000, the cap is $100,000. If they came to $250,000, the cap is $250,000.

Four things break through both limits entirely:

  • The indemnification promises in 7.1
  • Leaking confidential information (covered in Section 9)
  • Reckless carelessness or deliberate wrongdoing
  • Stealing or infringing the other side's intellectual property

In those four situations there is no cap and no exclusion — liability is unlimited.

Key Terms in Plain Language

TermWhat it actually means
IndemnifyTo cover someone else's costs when they get into legal trouble because of something you did. You pay so they don't have to.
DefendBeyond just paying — you hire the lawyers and actually fight the lawsuit on their behalf.
Hold harmlessA promise that the other side won't end up financially worse off. Usually bundled with "indemnify" as belt-and-suspenders wording.
Indemnifying PartyThe side doing the protecting and paying.
Indemnified PartiesThe side being protected — here, the company plus its executives, board members, staff, and agents.
Third-party claimA lawsuit or demand from someone outside the contract. This section does not cover the two parties suing each other.
RepresentationA statement of fact you assert is true right now ("we own this code").
WarrantyA guarantee about quality or performance, with a promise to make it right if it fails.
CovenantA promise to do — or not do — something going forward.
Gross negligenceFar worse than an honest mistake. Reckless disregard for obvious risks.
Willful misconductDoing something you knew was wrong, on purpose.
DeliverablesThe work products handed over under the contract — software, reports, designs, whatever was ordered.
InfringeUsing someone's patent, copyright, or trademark without permission.
MisappropriateTaking or using someone's trade secret or confidential information improperly.
Materially prejudicedGenuinely harmed in a way that matters — here, a late notice that actually hurt the defense, not one that was merely late.
Tender sole controlHand over full authority to manage the lawsuit and decide on settlement.
Not to be unreasonably withheldYou have veto power, but you can't use it arbitrarily. You need a legitimate reason to say no.
Indirect / consequential damagesKnock-on losses that flow from the problem rather than being the problem itself — a factory idled because a delivered part failed.
Incidental damagesSmall side costs of dealing with the problem, like shipping or inspection fees.
Special damagesLosses unique to your situation that wouldn't be obvious to an outsider.
Punitive / exemplary damagesMoney awarded to punish bad behavior, over and above the actual loss.
Loss of goodwillDamage to reputation and customer relationships.
Under any theory of liabilityThe limit applies no matter the legal label — breach of contract, negligence, or anything else.
Total cumulative liabilityEverything added together across the life of the contract, not a fresh limit per incident.
Fees paid or payableMoney already handed over plus money currently owed but not yet paid.

What to Watch For

  • The cap can be small. If the contract is low-value, $100,000 is the realistic ceiling on ordinary disputes — which may be far less than the harm a failure could cause.
  • "Lost profits" excluded is a big deal. For many business disputes, lost profits are the damage. Excluding them removes most of what you'd want to recover.
  • The carve-outs do the heavy lifting. The four exceptions in 7.3 are where real exposure lives. Whether a given dispute falls inside or outside them is often the whole fight.
  • Losing control of the defense has consequences. The other side picks the lawyers and the strategy. Your protection is limited to a veto on settlements that admit your fault or impose non-money obligations.
  • The IP exclusions can be broad in practice. Most delivered work gets modified or combined with other systems. Either can quietly void the IP protection.
This is a plain-language explanation of contract text, not legal advice. Specific wording, governing law, and the rest of the agreement can change how these provisions apply — consult a lawyer before relying on this summary.
